name: Tomas Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run operations at Lindenhof, a dairy and arable farm owned by Helga Brandt, who's 77 now and lets me get on with it. We milk 140 cows through two milking robots, and we grow maize, grass silage and some potatoes. My day starts on the tablet at six, checking which cows the robots flagged overnight for low yield or a high temperature. Then it's walking the sheds, a chat with the two lads, and fieldwork or meetings with the feed rep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzle of it: I ask the AI assistant to rework the feed ration when the silage tests come back, then I check it against what I see in the cows. What wears me out is the robots calling my phone at 2 a.m. because a cow's kicked the cup off. People think robots mean an easy life. They just move the work to the middle of the night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit, because I've always said the useful stuff is boring and the hype is nonsense. At the discussion group I'd say keep using what works and stop buying gadgets. Online I'd post about the dairy companies who promised miracles and delivered dashboards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me fine. I already use AI every day for rations and records, and that part would just carry on. Helga pays fairly, and I've got a few years left before I hand over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as now, and spend the spare time from the AI tools on things I've put off, like reseeding the bottom fields. I'd keep putting money aside, we've got about five months saved. I might teach the discussion group how I use the assistant for rations, for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. A bit flat, maybe, because I enjoy new things, but comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that would still worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helga's health, if I'm honest. She's 77, and her nephew in the city would inherit, and he's never mucked out a shed in his life. If the owner's nephew sold the farm, I'd be job hunting at 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the nephew sold the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are other dairy units around here, and a man who knows the robots is useful. I'd find something, maybe a step down. Ines, my wife, says I'd be a nightmare if I wasn't busy.

say: The **useful AI** is boring and the hype was always nonsense.
Farmers should keep what works and **stop buying gadgets**.
think: The plateau **suits me fine**, since I already use AI daily for rations.
My real risk is **Helga's nephew** selling the farm when she dies.
do: Keep running the farm and use spare time to **reseed the bottom fields**.
Teach the **discussion group** how to plan rations with an AI assistant, free.
feel: **Comfortable**, if a little **flat**, because he enjoys new things.
S0.quote: If the owner's nephew sold the farm, I'd be job hunting at 60.
fieldNote: He is already living the **robot dairy** life and has no illusions about it.
His one real worry is **ownership**: the elderly owner and a disinterested heir.
He is confident a man who **knows the robots** will always find work nearby.

steps.text: Reseed the bottom fields with the time saved by AI tools
Show the local discussion group how he plans feed rations with AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for farms, if the data stays with farmers. At the discussion group I'd push for a shared, public system for herd data, not one owned by the milk buyer. Online I'd say the time saved should go to shorter hours for farm workers, not bigger profits for processors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm on the right side of this. Farming is mostly hands-on, and the bits AI takes, like ration plans and ordering, I've already handed over. The lads on the yard are safe for a good while because robots for mucking out and fencing are years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the farm's paperwork, ordering and grant forms fully onto AI in the first six months. I'd do the short course in precision cropping at the college in the first winter. And I'd ask Helga to put 20,000 into a camera system that spots lame cows early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A bit guilty for being excited when I know others are worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the data should stay with farmers. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because whoever owns the herd data owns the farmer. The milk company already sees our yields every day, and if they get the AI too, they'll tell us what to feed and what we'll be paid. I've seen it happen with seed companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the two lads on the yard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonas, who's 22, to learn the robots inside out, because the fixers will be needed. The other lad, Karim, is better with animals than machines, and I'd tell him the herd still needs a good stockman. I'd make sure Helga knows they're both worth keeping.

say: This is **good news** for farms, if farmers keep the **data**.
Time saved should mean **shorter hours** for workers, not bigger profits for processors.
think: I'm **on the right side** of this, since farming is mostly hands-on.
Robots for **mucking out and fencing** are years away, so the yard is safe.
do: Move all paperwork, ordering and grants onto **AI within six months**.
Take the college's **precision cropping** short course in the first winter.
Ask Helga to invest **20,000 in cameras** that spot lame cows.
feel: **Excited**, with a little **guilt** about others who are worried.
S1.quote: Whoever owns the herd data owns the farmer.
fieldNote: He's an **early adopter** with a strong left-leaning view on **data ownership**.
His concern is **power**, not jobs: processors using AI to squeeze farmers.
He speaks up for the **younger workers** without being asked.

steps.text: Put all farm paperwork, orders and grant forms onto AI tools
Take the college's precision cropping course in the first winter
Ask Helga to spend 20,000 on lameness-spotting cameras
Push the discussion group for a shared public herd data system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules now: who owns the robots, who owns the data, and what happens to the people. I'd be writing to my representative in the first week. Online I'd be saying the government should tax the robot owners to pay for farm workers' pensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a mixed bag for me. The office side of my job goes in 2028, and frankly I'd welcome that. The worry is 2031, when I'm 63 and the robots can do the stock work, and Helga's nephew decides one robot company can run the whole place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd become the person who sets up and runs the new AI and robot systems at Lindenhof, so I'm the last one they'd let go. I'd ask Helga for a written contract to 2031 and a lump sum if the farm is sold. I'd also cut our spending, starting with the new car we'd planned, and put that 15,000 into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervy. I'm usually first through the gate with new things, but two years is fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between the thinking AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're the years when someone like me is worth the most. The AI plans everything, but a person still has to do the work in the shed until 2031. After that I'm 63, which is a bad age to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ines about the farm being sold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight that we'd likely need to live on her nursing wage for a few years. Ines would say fine, and then worry about it at 3 a.m. We'd talk about her working an extra shift, which I'd hate.

say: We need **rules now** on who owns the robots, the data and the people.
The government should **tax robot owners** to fund farm workers' pensions.
think: Losing the **office side** in 2028 would be welcome.
The danger is **2031**, at 63, when an heir hands everything to a robot firm.
do: Become the person who **runs the new systems**, so he's last to go.
Ask Helga for a **written contract** to 2031 and a payout if sold.
Drop the **new car** and put that 15,000 into savings.
feel: **Nervy**, because two years is fast even for someone who likes new things.
S2.quote: The AI plans everything, but a person still has to do the work in the shed until 2031. After that I'm 63, which is a bad age to start over.
fieldNote: He calls the **three-year gap** the peak of his value, then a cliff.
His fear is the **heir's decision**, not the technology itself.
Even an early adopter turns **cautious with money** when the clock is this short.

steps.text: Set up and run the new AI and robot systems at Lindenhof
Ask Helga for a contract to 2031 and a payout if sold
Drop the planned new car and save the 15,000 instead
Write to his representative about taxing robot owners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get the rules right, if politicians stop dithering. I'd join the farmworkers' union campaign for a robot levy. With friends I'd say don't panic, plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm in a decent position. I'm 63 when the thinking AI arrives and 66 when the robots take the stock work, and by then I'd want to ease off anyway. If I'm the one who brought the robots in, Helga or whoever owns Lindenhof will want me around to the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small side job now, advising other farms on milking robots and AI ration planning, maybe two days a month at 300 a day. I'd keep going at Lindenhof and add 250 a month to savings. And I'd help Jonas get his robot technician certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy way. Five years feels like a project, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why advise other farms rather than just keep your head down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advising farms is something I can carry past 66, sitting at a kitchen table with a farmer and a cup of coffee. Farmers trust another farmer, not a software rep. And the extra money would plug the pension gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you advise them to bring in robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them, yes, the ones who can't find staff. But I'd tell them to own the data and to keep at least one good stockman on. I'm not going to sell people something I'd regret.

say: Five years is **enough time** to get the rules right if politicians act.
Don't panic, **plan**, and back a **robot levy**.
think: At 63 and 66 I'm **in a decent position** for this timeline.
The person who **brought the robots in** gets kept to the end.
do: Start advising farms on **milking robots** two days a month at 300 a day.
Add **250 a month** to savings while staying at Lindenhof.
Help Jonas get his **robot technician certificate**.
feel: **Uneasy** but busy; five years feels like a **project**.
S3.quote: Advising farms is something I can carry past 66, sitting at a kitchen table with a farmer and a cup of coffee.
fieldNote: He turns the warning time into a **side business** that outlasts his job.
He keeps a **conscience** about what he would sell to other farmers.
His mood lifts noticeably with **five years**, because he can act first.

steps.text: Advise other farms on milking robots two days a month
Add 250 a month to savings while staying at Lindenhof
Join the farmworkers' union campaign for a robot levy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version we can actually handle well. At the discussion group I'd say let's spend the decade training young people for the robot side. Online I'd argue for public money for that training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it barely touches me. I'm 68 when the thinking AI arrives and 71 when robots come, and I'll have retired at 65. The robots will be for Jonas's generation to sort out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Lindenhof to 65 and keep bringing in AI tools as they prove themselves. I'd start the advice side gently in my last couple of years. And Ines and I would finally book the trip to see Felix in Canada.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit wistful that I'll miss the most interesting part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hand over to whoever replaces you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A notebook, believe it or not, with thirty years of which field floods and which cow line goes lame. The AI will know a lot, but not that the corner by the old oak always holds water. I'd type it up for them, actually, and feed it to the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every morning for a year, probably. Then I'd be bothering someone else's cows as an adviser.

say: This is the version we can **handle well** with training for young people.
Public money should fund **robot-side training** this decade.
think: It **barely touches me**, since I'll retire at 65.
The robots are for **Jonas's generation** to sort out.
do: Stay at Lindenhof to **65** and add AI tools as they prove out.
Start **advising farms** gently in the last couple of years.
Type up thirty years of **field notes** for his successor.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **wistful** about missing the most interesting part.

fieldNote: With ten years his **age** shields him almost entirely.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would land at Lindenhof right when I'm 63 and the nephew is in charge. What would help is a law that farm workers get a proper payout when a farm automates, linked to years worked. And a public scheme so older workers can draw a reduced pension early without being punished for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money the robots save. That's the whole question for me. If the money the robots save goes to the milk company and the investors, the countryside empties out.

headlineQuote: If the money the robots save goes to the milk company and the investors, the countryside empties out.
portrait: Tomas, 58, runs operations at a **140-cow robot dairy** for an elderly owner.
He uses **AI every day** for feed rations and records and enjoys the puzzle.
His progressive politics centre on **data ownership** and who keeps the money robots save.
His main risk is the owner's **heir selling** the farm when he's in his early sixties.
He grows calmer as warning time grows, turning it into a **side advice business**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots arriving at 63 and an heir who may sell to a robot firm.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving farm workers a **payout** linked to **years worked** when farms automate.
A **reduced early pension** for older workers without penalties.
